items.prompt: The whale shark is the largest fish in the ocean. How does it manage to grow to such an enormous size?

options.label: By filter-feeding on huge quantities of tiny plankton
options.feedback: Swimming slowly with its enormous mouth open, it strains vast amounts of water and keeps every tiny morsel that cannot pass through its gill rakers.

options.label: By hunting and swallowing other large sharks
options.feedback: A whale shark's mouth is built for straining tiny food from open water, not for seizing and swallowing prey anywhere near its own size.

options.label: By absorbing nutrients straight through its skin
options.feedback: Its thick skin is not built to absorb food; everything it eats still passes through a mouth and gut, just like any other fish.

options.label: By living for long stretches without eating at all
options.feedback: Going without food would only slow its growth; reaching such a size depends on feeding steadily, not on going hungry.

items.ok_line: An enormous mouth, straining an enormous amount of tiny food.
items.ko_line: Think about what a fish this size could possibly catch enough of to keep eating.
items.exp_title: Grown large on food too small to chase
items.exp_text: A whale shark swims slowly forward with its wide mouth open, drawing in huge volumes of seawater and pushing it back out through its gills, where bristly rakers trap plankton, small fish, and other tiny food. Because this food is so plentiful and needs no chase, no fight, and no speed to catch, the shark can spend its energy on growing rather than on hunting. That steady, effortless supply is what lets its body keep growing for years upon years of feeding this way.

items.prompt: The sailfish is the fastest fish in the ocean. What lets it reach such sudden bursts of speed?

options.label: It folds its fins flat into grooves and drives forward with a stiff tail
options.feedback: Tucking away every fin that would otherwise catch the water leaves a smooth, torpedo-shaped body for its powerful tail to drive through the water.

options.label: It keeps its tall sail fin raised at all times for extra thrust
options.feedback: The sail fin is folded down out of the way during a fast swim; raised, it would only add drag rather than speed.

options.label: It shoots a jet of water out from inside its body
options.feedback: That kind of jet propulsion belongs to a squid or an octopus; a sailfish drives itself forward with its tail instead.

options.label: It coats its skin in oil to reduce friction
options.feedback: No oily coating is what gives a sailfish its speed; the advantage comes from its shape and how it folds its fins away.

items.ok_line: Everything that could catch the water is tucked away before the tail drives forward.
items.ko_line: Think about what a fish covered in large fins would need to do with them before swimming at full speed.
items.exp_title: A shape built to slip through water
items.exp_text: Before a hard burst of speed, a sailfish folds its tall dorsal fin and its other fins down flat into grooves along its body, leaving almost nothing sticking out to drag against the water. Its stiff, crescent-shaped tail then sweeps side to side with great force, driving the now smoothly-shaped body forward with very little resistance to fight against. Folding away everything that could catch the water is what lets that powerful tail do its work with so little holding it back.

items.prompt: A sperm whale can dive deeper than almost any other diving animal. How does its body manage to cope down there?

options.label: Oxygen-rich muscle and a flexible ribcage let it endure the dive
options.feedback: Its muscles store extra oxygen for the dive, its heartbeat slows to make that oxygen last, and its ribcage flexes rather than snapping under the pressure.

options.label: It breathes underwater through its skin during the dive
options.feedback: A sperm whale still breathes air through its blowhole alone; no gas exchange happens through its skin while submerged.

options.label: It fills its body with extra gas to control its depth
options.feedback: Taking on extra gas would only make the crushing pressure at such depth more dangerous, not less.

options.label: Its body simply becomes numb to the pressure
options.feedback: Numbness would do nothing to protect the body from being crushed; the real defence lies in stored oxygen and a flexible skeleton.

items.ok_line: A stocked oxygen supply and a ribcage built to bend rather than break.
items.ko_line: Think about what the whale would need stored up before it even leaves the surface.
items.exp_title: Carrying its air supply in its own muscle
items.exp_text: Before diving, a sperm whale loads its blood and muscle with a protein that binds oxygen far more densely than blood alone can manage, giving it a reserve to draw on once it stops breathing. Its heartbeat slows dramatically during the dive to stretch that reserve further, and its ribcage is flexible enough to fold inward under pressure instead of cracking. That stored oxygen, spent slowly while the heart beats at its quietest, is what lets the whale keep functioning long after a shallow diver's air would have run out.

items.prompt: The Greenland shark can live longer than almost any other vertebrate animal. What allows it to survive for so long?

options.label: Its metabolism runs extremely slowly in the cold water it lives in
options.feedback: Cold water slows every chemical process inside its body, so growth, healing, and ageing all creep along at a fraction of the ordinary pace.

options.label: It stops ageing completely once it reaches adulthood
options.feedback: The shark's body does keep ageing throughout its life; what differs is simply how slowly that ageing proceeds.

options.label: It regrows an entirely new body every few years
options.feedback: No wholesale rebuilding of the body takes place; the same body simply changes at an unusually gentle pace.

options.label: It spends most of the year in a deep, motionless hibernation
options.feedback: It continues moving and hunting through the cold water rather than lying dormant for long stretches; the slowness lies in its metabolism, not in extended stillness.

items.ok_line: A body running its chemistry at an unusually gentle pace, start to finish.
items.ko_line: Think about how cold water might affect the speed of chemical processes happening inside any animal's body.
items.exp_title: A life lived at a slower pace
items.exp_text: The Greenland shark lives in near-freezing water, and cold slows down chemical reactions of every kind, including the ones that drive growth, repair, and the gradual wear of ageing inside a living body. With everything running at such a reduced pace, the shark grows only a very short distance each year and takes an unusually long time to reach maturity in the first place. Every process inside its body moves so gently that the years pass slowly, one long, cold season folding quietly into the next.

items.prompt: The ocean sunfish releases more eggs in one spawning than almost any other fish. Why does it release so many at once?

options.label: Because almost none of the drifting young will survive to adulthood
options.feedback: With no parent guarding any of them and countless predators along the way, releasing this many is what still leaves some chance that a few will survive.

options.label: The eggs are needed to feed other reef fish nearby
options.feedback: The eggs are not released as food for other fish; they are meant to develop and hatch, however few of them manage to.

options.label: All of the released eggs eventually fuse into one giant egg
options.feedback: The eggs stay separate and drift apart from one another; they never join together into a single mass.

options.label: Releasing many eggs at once helps the adult fish float better
options.feedback: Buoyancy for the adult sunfish has nothing to do with how many eggs it releases; the reason concerns the offspring's survival, not the parent's floating.

items.ok_line: Numbers standing in for the protection no parent is there to give.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to these eggs once they are released, with no parent watching over them.
items.exp_text: Once released into open water, sunfish eggs and the tiny larvae that hatch from them drift freely with the current, defenceless and exposed to countless predators and to simple starvation along the way. No parent stays behind to guard or feed them, so only a very small fraction of everything released will ever reach adulthood. With no other kind of protection available to them, releasing this many at once is simply what gives enough of these drifting young a chance to survive.

items.prompt: The mantis shrimp can strike hard enough to crack open a crab shell in an instant. How does it deliver such a powerful blow?

options.label: A spring-like arm stores energy, then releases it all in a sudden snap
options.feedback: A latch holds the folded arm under tension until it releases, letting stored energy snap the limb forward far quicker than a muscle could swing it directly.

options.label: It injects a fast-acting venom on contact
options.feedback: No venom is involved in the strike at all; the damage comes purely from the sheer mechanical force of the blow itself.

options.label: Sharp teeth similar to a shark's tear into the shell
options.feedback: A mantis shrimp has no teeth of that kind; it is a folded, club-like or spear-like limb that delivers the strike, not a bite.

options.label: One long, steady muscle contraction alone drives the strike
options.feedback: A single steady contraction could not produce a blow nearly this forceful; the strength instead comes from energy stored beforehand and released all at once.

items.ok_line: Energy stored first, then let go all at once in a single explosive snap.
items.ko_line: Think about what could make a strike far more forceful than a muscle contracting on its own.
items.exp_title: A snap built like a loaded spring
items.exp_text: Before it strikes, a mantis shrimp folds its clawed arm back and locks it in place with a latch, while a saddle-shaped structure inside the limb is bent and loaded with stored energy, much like a bow drawn tight before an arrow is loosed. When the latch releases, all of that stored energy is unleashed at once, snapping the arm forward far faster than the muscle pulling on it ever could by itself. Storing the energy first and releasing it all in a single instant is what turns a simple swing of the arm into an explosive strike.

items.prompt: The European eel makes one of the longest known migrations of any fish. Why does it leave the rivers where it has lived for years and swim far out into the open ocean?

options.label: It must return to the one region of ocean where its species has always spawned
options.feedback: Guided by an inherited instinct, the adult eel swims back toward the very stretch of open ocean where every generation of its kind has always bred.

options.label: Salt water triggers the sudden growth of legs for life on land
options.feedback: An eel remains a swimming fish throughout its life and grows no legs at any stage; its journey is entirely through water.

options.label: The open ocean is simply warmer and safer for laying eggs
options.feedback: Safety and warmth are not the deciding factor; the eel returns specifically to the one breeding ground its species has always used.

options.label: Crowding in the rivers forces young eels out to sea each year
options.feedback: It is the fully grown adult eel that undertakes this journey to breed, not young eels being pushed out by crowding in the rivers.

items.ok_line: The same distant breeding ground, returned to by every generation before it.
items.ko_line: Think about what an adult fish would need to do, once it is finally ready to breed.
items.exp_title: A journey back to where it all began
items.exp_text: A European eel spends most of its life growing in the rivers and lakes of Europe, far from the sea, but once mature it stops feeding, undergoes changes to its body suited for open-water swimming, and sets out across the Atlantic. It swims back toward one specific region of ocean where its species has always spawned, guided by instinct rather than by any landmark it could see along the way. That same current-riding journey, repeated by generation after generation, is what carries each new young eel back toward the rivers where the cycle can begin again.

items.prompt: Some starfish species can regrow into an entirely new animal from just a single severed arm. How is that possible?

options.label: The arm keeps enough of the central body attached to regrow the rest
options.feedback: As long as a fragment of the starfish's central disc stays attached to the arm, it carries the organs and tissue needed to rebuild everything missing.

options.label: The severed arm was already a hidden, fully-formed duplicate
options.feedback: Nothing complete is hidden inside a single arm beforehand; the missing body parts have to be built up gradually after the arm is severed.

options.label: Nearby starfish donate tissue to help the fragment regrow
options.feedback: No tissue is contributed by any other starfish; the regrowth relies entirely on what remains inside the surviving fragment itself.

options.label: Any cell in the surrounding seawater can turn into starfish tissue
options.feedback: Regeneration is not drawn from cells floating loose in the water; it depends on tissue already present inside the severed fragment.

items.ok_line: A fragment carrying just enough of the original body to build the rest again.
items.ko_line: Think about what part of the starfish's body a severed arm would need to keep attached to it.
items.exp_title: Rebuilt from what a fragment still holds
items.exp_text: In certain starfish species, each arm connects to a central disc that houses vital organs and a store of cells able to specialise into almost any tissue the body needs. If enough of that central disc stays attached when an arm is severed, those cells begin dividing and gradually forming the missing arms, organs, and structures around it. As long as enough of that central tissue survives attached to the fragment, the whole animal can eventually be built back up from it, piece by piece.

items.prompt: The toxin carried by a pufferfish is among the most dangerous in the sea. How does it cause paralysis in an animal that eats it?

options.label: It blocks the tiny channels nerve cells use to send signals
options.feedback: By plugging channels that normally let charged particles flow, the toxin stops a nerve cell from firing the electrical signal it needs to send.

options.label: It dissolves muscle tissue directly on contact
options.feedback: No muscle tissue is broken down by the toxin; the paralysis comes from silencing the nerves that control the muscles, not from harming the muscle itself.

options.label: It triggers a sudden allergic reaction confined to the heart
options.feedback: This is not an allergic response, and the effect is not limited to the heart; it interferes with nerve signals throughout the body.

options.label: It overstimulates nerves into uncontrollable spasms
options.feedback: The nerves are not overstimulated into firing too much; the toxin instead blocks them from firing at all.

items.ok_line: A blocked channel, and a nerve that can no longer send its signal onward.
items.ko_line: Think about what a nerve cell actually needs open in order to send a signal in the first place.
items.exp_title: A signal that never gets sent
items.exp_text: Nerve cells send their signals by letting charged particles flow briefly through tiny channels in their outer membrane, and this toxin fits precisely into those channels and plugs them shut. With the channels blocked, the electrical signal a nerve cell would normally send simply cannot form, and the message never reaches the muscle waiting at the other end. A nerve blocked this way falls silent, unable to pass its signal on any further.

items.prompt: The electric eel can produce one of the strongest shocks of any animal in the sea. How does its body generate that shock?

options.label: Many specialised cells stacked in a row discharge together like batteries in series
options.feedback: Each of these cells produces only a tiny voltage on its own, but stacked one after another and fired at the same moment, their combined charge adds together.

options.label: A single large internal organ acts like one giant battery
options.feedback: There is no single battery-like organ doing the work alone; the shock comes from many separate cells stacked together and firing as one.

options.label: Static electricity slowly builds up from swimming through the water
options.feedback: Swimming through water does not build up static charge in this way; the shock is actively generated by specialised cells within the eel's own body.

options.label: Venom-tipped spines along its body deliver an electric-like jolt
options.feedback: No spines or venom are involved at all; the shock is a purely electrical discharge generated internally, not something injected.

items.ok_line: Many small charges, added together by firing every cell at the very same moment.
items.ko_line: Think about what stacking many small batteries end to end would do to the total voltage.
items.exp_title: Small charges, added together at once
items.exp_text: Running along most of an electric eel's body are columns of specialised cells, each one able to produce only a small voltage on its own, arranged one after another much like batteries stacked end to end. When the eel's nervous system signals them to fire, every one of these cells discharges at exactly the same instant, and their small individual voltages add together along the length of the stack. Firing every cell together at that same moment is what turns many small charges into one combined jolt.
